message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Here's everything, roughly in order.

## What "lippage" means
**Lippage is when one tile sits slightly higher than the tile next to it, so the edges don't line up flat.** Run your hand across the joint and you'll feel a little step. It looks bad and catches socks and toes.

It's a particular risk with long tiles like 30 × 60 cm, because they're often very slightly bowed in the middle. That's why tile shops often say to offset them by **a third** rather than half in a brick pattern. A half offset lines up the high middle of one tile with the low end of the next.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain
Go for a **mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile.** It blends in, hides dirt, and won't show marks the way white or very pale grout does. Avoid white in a bathroom floor.

For extra stain resistance, consider a **stain-resistant or epoxy grout**. Epoxy is fiddlier to work with as a beginner. If you use standard cement-based grout, apply a grout sealer once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?
**Tile first, then fit the toilet.** That way the tiles run neatly underneath it with no awkward cuts around the pan, and the toilet sits on the finished floor at the right height for its seal and waste connection.

## How many boxes?

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| Area per tile | 0.3 m × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles needed | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 | 24 tiles |
| Plus 10% | 24 × 1.1 = 26.4 | 27 tiles |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4 | **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

**Buy 4 boxes.** It looks as if the tiles fit the room exactly, but they won't in practice:
- Grout joints add a few millimetres per tile, so the last row will need cutting.
- Walls are rarely perfectly straight or square.
- A brick pattern creates cuts at the edges of every other row.
- You'll need to cut around the toilet waste pipe.

Keep the spare tiles for future repairs, and check that all four boxes have the **same batch or shade number** on the label, since colours can vary between batches.

## Message to the neighbours
> Hi [Name],
>
> Just a heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor this Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise between about [9 am] and [12 pm]. We'll try to keep it as short as we can. Thank you so much for your patience, especially with the skip on the drive these past couple of weeks. It should all be finished soon!
>
> [Your names]

If you're on good terms with them, dropping off some biscuits or a bottle of wine buys a lot of goodwill.

## Three tips for a first floor
1. **Get the base right before anything else.** The floor underneath must be **solid, flat, clean and dry**. Tiles won't hide dips, and any flex will crack the grout. If it's a timber floor, it may need overboarding with tile backer board. Use a long spirit level and fix any dips first, because this is where most DIY floors go wrong.
2. **Dry-lay the tiles before you mix anything.** Lay a row or two out without adhesive to plan where the cuts will fall. Start from the centre or the most visible edge, usually the doorway, and avoid thin slivers at the door or along the most visible wall. Then mark guide lines on the floor.
3. **Work in small sections and control lippage as you go.** Mix small batches of adhesive and use the trowel size the tile shop recommends. Back-butter each large tile with a thin layer on its underside for good coverage. **Tile levelling clips** are cheap and make it much easier to keep the tiles flat. Check each tile with a level as you lay it. Leave a small gap at the walls for expansion, which the skirting will cover, and keep off the floor for at least 24 hours.

It's slower and more fiddly than the videos make it look, so give yourself more time than you think you'll need. You'll do fine.
